<ChapterHeader title="Workspaces" />

<Lead>
  A workspace is a shared encrypted folder: a named group that owns a tree of files, with a
  roster of members who can read, write, or administer depending on their role. Technically
  it's a keyring on the owner's PDS plus a collaborative proposal protocol that lets members
  edit without needing write access to the owner's repository.
</Lead>

## When to use a workspace (vs. a one-to-one grant)

If you want to share a single file with one other person, [grants](/docs/sdk/sharing) are the
lighter tool: one record per sharer, recipient decrypts directly from the sharer's PDS, no
group state. Grants scale poorly though. Adding a new person to a folder of 200 files means
200 new grant records. Removing someone means deleting every grant they received.

A workspace inverts that. The content key for each file is wrapped under a single **group
key**, and the group key is wrapped to each member individually. Adding a member is one
operation regardless of how many files are in the workspace. Removing a member rotates the
group key once; future uploads are inaccessible to them automatically.

Use workspaces for anything ongoing and multi-party: a family photo album, a research team's
working files, a writing group's drafts.

## Create a workspace

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="create.ts" code={createWorkspace} />

`createWorkspace` generates a fresh group key inside WASM, wraps it to the caller's public
key with the `manager` role (owners are always managers of their own workspace), writes the
`app.opake.keyring` record to the caller's PDS, and writes the workspace root directory
entry. The returned `key` is the group key bytes; you can hold onto it for immediate use, but
you don't need to store it anywhere. Opake re-resolves via `keyringUri` on every subsequent
operation.

## List and watch workspaces

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="list.ts" code={listAndWatchWorkspaces} />

`listWorkspaces` fetches from the indexer and decrypts workspace names inline. It also
bootstraps the in-memory `WorkspaceKeeper`, so `watchWorkspaces` subscribers receive
incremental updates from SSE events after the first call without the list round-tripping the
indexer again.

`@opake/react` wraps this pattern as `useWorkspaces` with the subscription lifecycle handled.
See [React bindings](/docs/react/overview) when those pages land.

## Add a member

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="add-member.ts" code={addWorkspaceMember} />

The invitee needs an Opake public key published on their PDS. If `resolveHandleAndPublicKey`
fails with `RecipientNotReady`, it means the target has a valid atproto identity but hasn't
logged into Opake yet and therefore has no `app.opake.publicKey/self` record. You can queue a
pending invite and wait for them to sign up; see [Sharing](/docs/sdk/sharing) for the
pending-share mechanic, which applies the same way to workspace invites.

Three roles exist:

- **`manager`**: can add or remove members, change workspace metadata, and edit files like any editor.
- **`editor`**: can read everything, upload new documents, and propose edits to existing ones.
- **`viewer`**: can read but not write. Proposals from viewers are rejected by the owner daemon.

Roles are enforced at the proposal-apply layer, not at the crypto layer. A viewer has the group
key (that's what membership means) and can decrypt. Role enforcement stops them from *writing*
valid proposals that the owner would accept. If your threat model requires a viewer who can't
see content at all, they shouldn't be a workspace member.

## Remove a member

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="remove-member.ts" code={removeWorkspaceMember} />

Removing a member is the expensive operation by design. When the owner initiates it:

1. A fresh group key is generated inside WASM.
2. Every remaining member's entry in the keyring is re-wrapped to the new key.
3. The previous rotation's wrapped keys are archived into `keyHistory` on the keyring record
   so the remaining members can still decrypt older documents (which were wrapped under the
   old key).
4. The `rotation` counter increments.
5. Future uploads use the new key.

The removed member keeps whatever they already decrypted or cached locally. Rotation prevents
*new* access, not retroactive access. If the threat model requires forward secrecy for
existing documents, the owner has to re-upload them after rotation. Opake doesn't do this
automatically.

## Leave a workspace

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="leave.ts" code={leaveWorkspace} />

The member-side counterpart to being removed. Opting out goes through the same proposal path:
the member writes a `keyringUpdate` with `actionType: "leave"` on their own PDS, the owner's
daemon picks it up, and the standard rotate-and-re-wrap flow runs.

Owners can't `leaveWorkspace` on their own workspace. Depending on the membership list they'd
either leave themselves as the only member, or orphan the workspace entirely. To dissolve an
owned workspace, remove the other members and then delete the keyring record directly.

## How proposals work

Members who aren't the owner can't write to the owner's repository. The PDS auth model doesn't
allow cross-account writes. So when an editor renames a file in a workspace, or uploads a new
document, or moves a directory around, Opake doesn't touch the owner's PDS directly. Instead
it writes a **proposal record** on the member's own PDS, describing the intended change.

<CodeBlock language="typescript" title="proposal-flow.ts" code={proposalFlow} />

The owner's daemon (or wherever the owner's Opake instance is running) periodically scans for
pending proposals against workspaces it owns. For each, it checks the proposer's role
(`viewer` → reject; `editor`/`manager` → accept), applies the change as a canonical record on
the owner's repository, and deletes the proposal from the member's PDS.

The proposal record types are:

- **`app.opake.documentUpdate`**: proposed document changes. Content updates, metadata edits,
  adoption (claiming an existing member-uploaded document into the owner's canonical tree).
- **`app.opake.directoryUpdate`**: proposed structure changes. Add entry, remove entry, move
  entry, create directory, delete directory, rename directory.
- **`app.opake.keyringUpdate`**: proposed membership changes. Add member, remove member,
  update role, rename workspace, update description, leave.

From your application's perspective, this is mostly invisible. You call `fm.upload(...)` or
`fm.move(...)`, the WASM side figures out whether the caller is the owner and routes
accordingly, and you get a `MutationResult` back that tells you whether the write was applied
directly or proposed.

## Reading `MutationResult`

<CodeBlock
  language="typescript"
  title="mutation-result.ts"
  code={mutationResultHandling}
/>

`proposed: true` means the write is pending apply on the owner's side. The returned URI is the
proposal record on the caller's own PDS, not the target document or directory on the owner's
PDS (which doesn't exist yet).

For optimistic UI, render the change immediately with a "pending" affordance. When the owner
applies, the SSE consumer fires a tree update on the target directory and the pending marker
can come off. If the owner rejects or if the daemon hasn't run in a while, the pending marker
stays until the proposal is applied or cancelled.

## A note on the indexer

Workspaces are discovered via the Opake [indexer](/docs/glossary#indexer), not the PDS firehose
directly. `listWorkspaces` calls `/api/keyrings` with the caller's DID as a filter; the
indexer returns every keyring where the caller appears in the member list (including
keyrings the caller owns, since owners are always listed as the first member).

If you're running against a self-hosted indexer instead of the default, set the URL via the
`OPAKE_INDEXER_URL` env var at build time, or call `opake.setIndexerUrl()` at runtime. See
the account config mechanic in [Authentication](/docs/sdk/authentication) for how a user's
preferred indexer syncs across their devices.
